claim: Eisenberg's peer-reviewed paper (Accident Analysis & Prevention 36(4):637-647, 2004; US, 48 states, 1975-2000) finds that rain's crash effect grows with the time since the last precipitation. 1 cm of precipitation raises the state-day fatal crash rate by about 3% when exactly 2 days have passed since the last precipitation, and by about 9% when more than 20 days have passed. The abstract says the same pattern holds for non-fatal crashes. For scoring: the dry-spell length before today's rain should multiply the rain effect.
numbers: about 3% per 1 cm at exactly 2 days since last precipitation; about 9% per 1 cm at more than 20 days; fatal crashes, 1975-2000, 48 states
surfaces: all (state-level totals, no surface breakdown)
short_quote: by about 9% if more than 20 days have passed
source: The mixed effects of precipitation on traffic crashes (Eisenberg, Accid Anal Prev 2004), PubMed abstract

claim: The same paper finds a strong negative lagged effect: heavy rain yesterday means fewer crashes today, on average. It does not settle the cause. It offers two explanations: rain clears oil that builds up on roads during dry periods, or people become conditioned to drive more safely in wet conditions. A model should therefore include yesterday's rain or recent rain totals with a negative sign on top of today's rain, and the write-up should not present the oil mechanism as proven.
surfaces: all
short_quote: if it rained a lot yesterday, then on average, today there are fewer crashes
source: The mixed effects of precipitation on traffic crashes (Eisenberg, Accid Anal Prev 2004), PubMed abstract

claim: The 2003 UC Berkeley press release on the study gives slightly different numbers from the paper's abstract. Per centimeter of rain today: no added fatal-crash risk if it also rained yesterday, 3.7% more if 2 days have passed since the last rain, and 9.2% more at 21 days, which it calls about 2.5 times the 2-day risk. It names two explanations. Oil and debris build up in dry weather and wash off by the second day of rain. Drivers are out of practice after a dry spell and may adapt by day two or three. The release suggests warning signs and lower speed limits for the first rain after a dry spell, which supports the project's alert use case.
numbers: 0% added fatal risk if it rained yesterday; +3.7% at 2 days since last rain; +9.2% at 21 days (about 2.5x); per 1 cm of rain
surfaces: all
short_quote: Oil and debris accumulate on the road when it hasn't rained for a while
source: Rain is more lethal for drivers after a long dry spell (UC Berkeley News, Oct 31, 2003)

claim: Per the Berkeley release, on a given day each centimeter of precipitation raises fatal crash risk by about 1% and non-fatal crash risk by 11% (non-fatal data: 36.4 million crashes, 17 states, 1990-1999). The release says precipitation had a larger impact on non-fatal crashes overall. The DFW table counts every severity, so its overall rain effect may be larger than the fatal-only figures. The source gives no non-fatal dry-spell percentages, so the 3.7% and 9.2% figures cannot be called a floor for DFW.
numbers: about 1% per cm for fatal crashes; 11% per cm for nonfatal crashes; 36.4 million nonfatal crashes, 17 states, 1990-1999
surfaces: all
short_quote: for nonfatal crashes, the increased risk is 11 percent
source: Rain is more lethal for drivers after a long dry spell (UC Berkeley News, Oct 31, 2003)

claim: An independent city-scale study backs the dry-spell effect. Keay and Simmonds (Melbourne, Australia, 1987-2002, crash counts normalized by traffic volume) found that rain after a dry spell has a larger effect as the spell gets longer, and that the first-rain impact grows with both spell length and rain amount. The effect shows up more clearly when broken down by rain class. This supports an interaction between dry days before rain and rain amount, rather than a simple add-on. The abstract gives no percentage for the dry-spell effect.
numbers: Melbourne, 1987-2002; no dry-spell percentage given in abstract
surfaces: all (metropolitan roads, no surface breakdown)
short_quote: Rainfall occurring after a dry spell has an enhanced effect on the volume-normalised accident count
source: Road accidents and rainfall in a large Australian city (Keay & Simmonds, Accid Anal Prev 38(3):445-454, 2006), PubMed abstract

claim: Andrey and Yagar (Calgary and Edmonton, 1979-1983, 169 rain events, over 15,000 crashes, matched-sample method) found crash risk during rainfall about 70% above normal. Risk returned to normal as soon as the rain stopped, even though roads stayed wet. For daily scores this means that being rained on is what counts, not a lingering wet road. A dry day after a rainy day should not get much extra risk. Note that daily DFW rain totals cannot show how many hours it actually rained.
numbers: +70% crash risk during rainfall; 169 rain events; over 15,000 crashes; 1979-1983
surfaces: all (urban roads in two Canadian cities)
short_quote: accident risk returns to normal as soon as the rainfall has ended
source: A temporal analysis of rain-related crash risk (Andrey & Yagar, Accid Anal Prev 25(4):465-472, 1993), PubMed abstract

claim: A Caltrans pavement study (more than 50,000 skid tests on California freeways, 1988-2008) supports a pavement mechanism for the dry-spell effect. Its skid-resistance model was fitted on asphalt concrete pavement data and found that wet-pavement skid resistance (SN40) drops as dry periods get longer. SN40 also drops with higher temperature and higher traffic (ADT), and the shoulder lane runs lower than average. The report links skid resistance to the number of dry months before the last significant rain. Two cautions: the time scale is months, not days, and the study measures friction, not crashes. Open-graded asphalt resurfacing cut wet-related collisions by 10-73%.
numbers: more than 50,000 skid observations, 1988-2008; SN40 below 30 deemed unacceptable by most DOTs; OGAC resurfacing reduced collisions 10-73 percent
surfaces: asphalt concrete (the deterioration model used asphalt concrete pavement on four California routes); open-graded asphalt for the collision part
short_quote: SN40 decreases with the increased length of dry periods.
source: Evaluation of Traffic and Environment Effects on Skid Resistance and Safety Performance of Rubberized Open Graded Asphalt Concrete (Caltrans DRISI Research Results, Task 1118, Sept 2009)

claim: An FHWA Long-Term Pavement Performance paper (263 skid tests, 78 sites, 28 states) cites earlier research on two points. Friction is often poor after a long lack of rain, because surface contamination likely lubricates the tire-aggregate contact. Seasonal swings in skid resistance were generally larger on asphalt concrete than on portland cement concrete, which the authors put down to asphalt's greater sensitivity to solar heating. The paper's own data point to temperature, not snow-removal operations, as the cause of seasonal variation. This supports testing whether first-rain and hot-then-rain effects are larger on asphalt-type surfaces than on concrete. It is evidence about friction, not crash counts.
numbers: 263 skid tests at 78 sites in 28 states; mean and median skid number 47 (SD 8.25); model monthly reductions 0.0 (July) to 5.8 (January)
surfaces: asphalt concrete vs portland cement concrete (larger seasonal changes on asphalt); dry-spell contamination statement applies to pavements generally
short_quote: poor friction performance often results after a long lack of rain
source: Investigation of Seasonal Variation in Pavement Friction Using the DataPave 3.0 Database (McDonald, Crowley, Turochy), in FHWA-HRT-06-109, Sept 2006

claim: Wet friction depends on two scales of pavement texture, and which one matters depends on speed. Microtexture (wavelength < 0.5 mm, from the surface of the aggregate particles in the asphalt or concrete) sets the friction level and dominates at low speed. Macrotexture (0.5 to 50 mm, from the aggregate size, shape and gradation of asphalt mixes and from concrete finishing such as dragging, tining or grooving) drains water and corresponds to the hysteresis part of friction. Hysteresis grows exponentially with speed and above 65 mi/hr (105 km/hr) accounts for over 95 percent of friction (PIARC, 1987). By our own inference, not the guide's: macrotexture loss probably matters most on high-speed roads and microtexture more on lower-speed roads.
numbers: microtexture wavelength < 0.5 mm; macrotexture 0.5 to 50 mm; above 65 mi/hr (105 km/hr) hysteresis is over 95 percent of friction
surfaces: all (asphalt and concrete); speed-dependent
short_quote: Hysteresis increases with speed exponentially, and at speeds above 65 mi/hr (105 km/hr) accounts for over 95 percent of the friction
source: NCHRP Web-Only Document 108: Guide for Pavement Friction (Hall et al., NCHRP Project 01-43, Feb 2009; sponsored by AASHTO with FHWA)

claim: A very thin water film is enough to cut friction a lot, and light rain is enough to make one. About 0.05 mm (0.002 in) of water can lower friction 20 to 30% below dry. A film like that is likely in any hour with at least 0.01 in of rain, which is the project's own rain-day threshold. The film matters little below 20 mph but a great deal above 40 mph. Friction falls exponentially as the film thickens. Hydroplaning, where friction drops to near zero, needs thick water (from heavy rain, poor drainage, or ruts and puddles) plus high speed. Contact can be lost at 40 to 45 mph on puddles about 1 in deep and 30 ft long. Larger macrotexture means the water must be deeper before hydroplaning starts.
numbers: 0.002 in (0.05 mm) water gives 20 to 30 percent friction loss; film likely in any hour with at least 0.01 in (0.25 mm) of rain; WFT effect minimal below 20 mi/hr and pronounced above 40 mi/hr; hydroplaning at 40 to 45 mi/hr on puddles about 1 in deep and 30 ft long
surfaces: all; hydroplaning risk is highest on high-speed roads with ruts or poor drainage
short_quote: as little as 0.002 in (0.05 mm) of water on the pavement surface can reduce the coefficient of friction by 20 to 30 percent
source: NCHRP Web-Only Document 108: Guide for Pavement Friction (Hall et al., 2009)

claim: Lower friction means more wet-weather crashes. The guide summarizes many studies. Gothie (1996): wet crash rates rose at least 50 percent from sections with SFC > 0.60 to sections with SFC < 0.50, and a 0.05 drop in SFC raised crash risk and severity about 50 percent. Separately, French research on the Bordeaux Ring Road (Larson, 1999) found a five-fold rise in wet crash rates for the same SFC drop. On England's M4, resurfacing (friction 0.40 to 0.55 at 50 mi/hr) cut wet crashes 63 percent and dry crashes 28 percent. A Texas study of 571 sites (McCullough and Hankins, 1966) recommended a minimum friction coefficient of 0.40 at 30 mi/hr. The guide says the friction-to-wet-crash relationship is site-specific and must be developed for the sites in a given network. Using road-level random effects is our inference from that.
numbers: wet crash rate up at least 50 percent from SFC > 0.60 to SFC < 0.50; a 0.05 drop in SFC raised crash risk and severity about 50 percent; resurfacing (friction 0.40 to 0.55) cut wet crashes 63 percent and dry crashes 28 percent; Texas 571 sites, minimum 0.40 at 30 mi/hr
surfaces: all
short_quote: wet crash rates increased by at least 50 percent when moving from a section with a Sideway Force Coefficient (SFC) greater than 0.60
source: NCHRP Web-Only Document 108: Guide for Pavement Friction (Hall et al., 2009), chapter on wet-weather crashes and pavement friction

claim: Polishing removes friction differently on the two surface types. On asphalt, the hardness and mineral makeup of the coarse aggregate decide how much traffic polishes the microtexture. A concrete surface is mostly mortar and starts with no exposed coarse aggregate, so the polish resistance of the fine aggregate matters most there; coarse aggregate counts only once it is exposed. After construction, traffic shear forces can break down aggregate and remove macrotexture. Elsewhere the guide tracks friction loss against pavement age and groups friction design by speed and traffic, so age and ADT are plausible proxies for lost friction. That proxy use is our inference.
surfaces: asphalt (HMA) vs portland cement concrete
short_quote: For concrete mixes, because the surface is composed primarily of mortar and is initially devoid of coarse aggregates, the polishing resistance of fine aggregates
source: NCHRP Web-Only Document 108: Guide for Pavement Friction (Hall et al., 2009), aggregate properties section

claim: On California urban freeways carrying more than 60,000 vehicles a day, transversely tined (TT) concrete had 95 crashes per 100 million vehicle miles, longitudinally tined (LT) concrete 100 and asphalt 108, for all crashes in all weather. The TT sections there were bridge decks only. On the same freeways the wet-to-dry ratio was 0.16 for LT and about 0.20 for both TT and asphalt. On Wisconsin rural freeways under 60,000 vehicles a day, the wet-to-dry ratio was 0.16 for TT and 0.23 for asphalt. With snow and ice included, asphalt did better: 1.26 (1.23 in the body text) for asphalt vs. 1.50 for TT. The data come from California and Wisconsin, not Texas.
numbers: 95 vs 100 vs 108 crashes per 100 million VMT (TT, LT, asphalt); wet-to-dry 0.16 (TT) vs 0.23 (asphalt); (wet + snow/ice)-to-dry 1.50 (TT) vs 1.26 (asphalt)
surfaces: transversely tined PCC, longitudinally tined PCC, asphalt; freeways
short_quote: TT had a lower crash rate than LT which, in turn, had a lower crash rate than asphalt pavements
source: Wet Pavement Crash Study of Longitudinally Tined PCC Pavements, Transversely Tined PCC Pavements and Asphalt Pavements (Drakopoulos and Kuemmel, Marquette University, July 2004)

claim: Tined concrete in Texas can lose much of its texture under traffic, and how much varies widely. Early Texas studies expected 25 to 35 percent wear. 1984 re-measurements of the 1971-73 experimental texture sections on SH 6 near Bryan and IH 10 near Van Horn found wear from 22 to 74 percent of the original texture depth. The smaller losses came mostly from surfaces with small initial textures, usually not tined. One longitudinally tined IH 10 section went from 0.065 in to 0.017 in after 17 million vehicle passes. Texas research judged a texture depth of about 0.035 in desirable for reducing rural wet-weather crashes, and the spec required an average of 0.060 in. Older, heavily trafficked concrete may therefore have much less texture than when built.
numbers: expected wear 25 to 35 percent; measured wear 22 to 74 percent of original; desirable texture depth about 0.035 in; spec 0.060 in average
surfaces: portland cement concrete (tined), Texas
short_quote: Attachments III and IV indicate the wear down can be as low as 22 percent
source: A Review of Tines Texturing of Portland Cement Concrete Paving, Research Report 187-10 (K.D. Hankins, Texas State Dept. of Highways and Public Transportation with FHWA, June 1984)

claim: Crash risk rises with rain intensity and falls once the rain stops. Across the contiguous US, using high-resolution radar, the relative risk of a fatal crash during precipitation was 1.34 overall. It rose from about 1.27 in light precipitation to 2.46 in heavy precipitation. The authors note that much of the risk applies only while precipitation is actually falling. A daily rain total from one airport gauge will therefore blur both the intensity and the timing of risk.
numbers: overall RR 1.343 (95% CI 1.315 to 1.371); light 1.27 (1.29 in Discussion); heavy 2.46 (CI 2.29 to 2.63)
surfaces: all (not split by surface)
short_quote: nearly doubling from 1.27 during light precipitation to 2.46 during heavy precipitation
source: Precipitation and Fatal Motor Vehicle Crashes: Continental Analysis with High-Resolution Radar Data (Stevens, Schreck, Saha, Bell, Kunkel), Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society 100(8), 2019

claim: Friction follows a seasonal and dry-spell cycle: highest in winter, lowest in summer. Dust, tire and road debris build up on the surface, mostly in summer. At the first rain after a dry period they mix with water into a viscous lubricant that cuts friction. Runoff then washes them off and friction recovers. This gives a physical reason for a 'days since rain' or dry-spell effect, and it could be stronger after long dry, hot spells. It is a short conference abstract with a lab test only, and it gives no crash numbers.
surfaces: all (lab specimens; not split by surface type)
short_quote: At the first rain after a dry period, these particles are mixed with water drops and form a viscous lubricant.
source: Laboratory test to evaluate the effect of contaminants on road skid resistance (M.T. Do, V. Cerezo, H. Zahouani; Ifsttar and Ecole Centrale de Lyon), 40th Leeds-Lyon Symposium on Tribology, 2013 (abstract)

claim: TTI's 'Get a Grip' note (Aug 6, 2013) defines bleeding and flushing as hot weather pushing asphalt binder up onto the pavement surface, which makes the surface slicker and can cause sliding. Its case is a flushed seal coat at the busy US 59 / Loop 287 interchange in Lufkin, worn down by heavy, fast truck traffic. There, low friction in rain led to vehicles sliding off the road. A fine permeable friction course was laid over it, which the note says is 'particularly useful where wet-weather accidents occur.' The TxDOT district construction director said slide-offs then went down but did not stop. The evidence is about a seal coat (surface treatment) at a high-shear interchange, not thick hot-mix asphalt.
numbers: No crash counts given. The fix was laid at the start of summer 2011, which the note calls one of Texas's hottest summers on record, with a record number of 100-degree-plus days.
surfaces: Seal coat / surface treatment (TxDOT surface-treated group); high-shear interchange ramps
short_quote: When it rained, friction was low, which resulted in vehicles sliding off the road.
source: Get a Grip: New Fine PFC Offsets Bleeding, Flushing on Roadways (Texas A&M Transportation Institute, Aug 6, 2013). Opened from the Internet Archive copy of Sep 7, 2017, because the live URL https://tti.tamu.edu/2013/08/06/get-a-grip now returns 404

claim: A TTI research engineer describes flushing as excess binder pushed up to the surface until it covers the aggregate. The result is a black, often sticky surface that can lose skid resistance. The article calls this a common problem with Texas seal coats and surface treatments and sets it in the Texas summer. TxDOT tested ultra-high-pressure water blasting to remove the extra binder. The Texas Tech lead researcher said it restored the seal coat's macrotexture and improved the microtexture of the exposed aggregate. The article does not give friction numbers.
numbers: Water jets at 36,000 psi; half-mile test section in Grimes County; about 186,000 lane miles maintained by TxDOT; over $2 billion a year in maintenance spending (background figures, not crash data)
surfaces: Seal coats and surface treatments (thin-surfaced roads)
short_quote: QUOTE WITHHELD under the one-short-quote rule for copyrighted non-federal pages. Paraphrase: excess binder covers the aggregate, leaving a black, sticky surface that can lose skid resistance.
source: Removing Excess Asphalt: Initial test of ultra-high-pressure water blasting a success (Texas Transportation Researcher, Vol. 46 No. 2, June 2010, TTI). Opened from the Internet Archive copy of Feb 16, 2025; the live page now returns 404

claim: TxDOT Project Summary 0-5230 (Texas Tech TechMRT, completed 8-31-06) reports general agreement that bleeding and flushing both come from excess asphalt binder filling the voids between aggregate particles. It lists five contributing factor groups: aggregate, binder, traffic, environmental and construction. It distinguishes 'bleeding' (an active problem needing immediate, sometimes emergency, maintenance) from 'flushed' (the past-tense state, usually not urgent). Flushed pavement calls for treatment when the surface is slippery, skid resistance is low, or there is rutting with water collecting in the wheel paths. The study says binder quality in general, and temperature susceptibility in particular, are not the dominant factors behind current bleeding and flushing. More than 120 TxDOT staff were interviewed, with over 2,500 combined years of experience.
numbers: More than 120 TxDOT staff interviewed (over 2,500 combined years of experience); project completed 8-31-06
surfaces: Seal coats and surface treatments on TxDOT asphalt pavements
short_quote: QUOTE WITHHELD under the one-short-quote rule for copyrighted non-federal pages. Paraphrase: flushed-surface treatment thresholds include slippery surface, low skid resistance, and rutting with water accumulating in the wheel paths.
source: Project Summary 0-5230: Short Term Solutions to 'Bleeding' Asphalt Pavements (TxDOT Research and Technology Implementation Office; Texas Tech TechMRT)

claim: TxDOT Project Summary 0-5230 says intersections can be especially problematic. Heavy vehicles turning and braking can make aggregate roll, which leads to aggregate loss and bleeding of the seal. Concentrated heavy traffic at intersections may push aggregate in too deep, which leads to flushing of the binder.
surfaces: Seal coats / surface treatments, especially at intersections and other places with heavy-vehicle braking and turning
short_quote: QUOTE WITHHELD under the one-short-quote rule for copyrighted non-federal pages. Paraphrase: heavy-vehicle turning and braking at intersections causes aggregate loss and bleeding; concentrated heavy traffic causes embedment and flushing.
source: Project Summary 0-5230: Short Term Solutions to 'Bleeding' Asphalt Pavements (TxDOT)

claim: The FHWA LTPP Distress Identification Manual glossary (Fifth Revised Edition, FHWA-HRT-13-092, May 2014) describes bleeding as a film of bituminous material on the pavement surface. The film creates a shiny, glass-like reflective surface that may be tacky to the touch in warm weather.
surfaces: Asphalt (bituminous) surfaces
short_quote: shiny, glass-like reflective surface that may be tacky to the touch in warm weather
source: Distress Identification Manual for the Long-Term Pavement Performance Program (Fifth Revised Edition, FHWA-HRT-13-092), Glossary

claim: FHWA Technical Advisory T 5040.36 (June 17, 2005; page updated June 27, 2017) gives microtexture as wavelengths of 1 micrometre to 0.5 mm and macrotexture as 0.5 mm to 50 mm. It states that both are needed for wet pavement friction at low and high speeds. It cites Swedish research that, on worn pavements, crash rates increase on days with 10 mm or more of rain. It says concrete typically needs a supplemental treatment, such as transverse tining, to get adequate macrotexture. Superpave-designed HMA generally gives adequate macrotexture and microtexture without supplemental treatments.
numbers: Microtexture 1 µm to 0.5 mm; macrotexture 0.5 mm to 50 mm; crash rates rise on worn pavements on days with at least 10 mm of rain (Swedish research)
surfaces: All (asphalt and concrete); the 10 mm finding applies to worn pavements
short_quote: Both microtexture and macrotexture are necessary to provide wet pavement friction at low and high speed conditions.
source: FHWA Technical Advisory T 5040.36: Surface Texture for Asphalt and Concrete Pavements (June 17, 2005; page updated June 27, 2017)

claim: In FHWA-HRT-06-109, Paper 3 (Mark P. McDonald, Auburn University) cites Burchett and Rizenbergs: skid resistance follows an annual sinusoidal cycle, and the changes were generally greater on asphalt concrete than on PCC. McDonald suggests this is because asphalt is nearly a black body and much more sensitive to solar radiation than PCC. His own DataPave 3.0 analysis found that snowfall did not organize the friction data while temperature began to. Temperature effects explained only about 5.7% of the variance in skid numbers (R-squared about 0.057). The paper's introduction gives Alabama figures: 22% of all crashes and 15% of fatal crashes happen on wet pavement, though roads are wet only about 4% of the time.
surfaces: Asphalt concrete vs portland cement concrete
short_quote: The changes in asphalt concrete surfaces were generally greater than the changes in portland cement concrete (PCC).
source: Paper 3: Investigation of Seasonal Variation in Pavement Friction Using the DataPave 3.0 Database (M. P. McDonald, Auburn University), in FHWA-HRT-06-109 LTPP student papers

claim: Concrete reacts to heat differently. It does not bleed binder. Its main heat failure is the 'blow-up', where a slab expands at a joint or crack that has let in moisture, then buckles and shatters. Nebraska DOT says this usually happens on very hot afternoons, typically at 90 F or hotter. Blow-ups are more common in older concrete and after a wet spring followed by very hot weather. On asphalt overlays, the pavement pushes up into a bump instead. This is a sudden local structural hazard, not a loss of friction in rain. FHWA's distress glossary defines a blowup as localized upward movement or shattering of a slab at a transverse joint or crack.
numbers: Typically on afternoons at 90 F or hotter; blow-ups range from a few inches to over a foot; at least a dozen in one Nebraska district at the time of writing
surfaces: Jointed concrete mainly; asphalt-over-concrete overlays can push up into bumps
short_quote: QUOTE WITHHELD under the one-short-quote rule for copyrighted non-federal pages. Paraphrase: blow-ups usually occur on afternoons of 90 degrees or hotter, and more often after a wet spring followed by heat.
source: High Summer Temperatures Cause Pavement Blow-Ups (Nebraska Department of Transportation)

claim: On seal coat (chip seal) surfaces, asphalt bleeding can drastically cut skid resistance whatever the quality of the aggregate. How much grip a seal coat has depends heavily on the quality of its design and construction. Of the seal coat grades studied, Grade 3 gave a higher mean profile depth (texture) and skid number than the other grades. The study looked at 35 surface-treated sections and 35 asphalt-mix sections in Texas.
numbers: 35 test sections of asphalt mixtures and 35 test sections of surface-treated roads
surfaces: seal coat / surface treatment (compared with hot-mix asphalt)
short_quote: Asphalt bleeding can drastically reduce the skid resistance on seal coat surface regardless of the quality of aggregate.
source: TxDOT Project Summary 0-6746: Validation of TxDOT Flexible Pavement Skid Prediction Model (TTI, completed 7-31-2015)

claim: TTI describes a heat-then-rain sequence on a seal coat. Hot weather made the asphalt binder expand up onto the surface (bleeding and flushing), which left it slicker. When it later rained, friction was low and vehicles slid off the road. This is one case, not a crash-rate study: a heavily used truck exit at the US 59 / Loop 287 interchange in Lufkin, where the sealcoat had bled and flushed under heavy, fast truck traffic.
surfaces: seal coat (sealcoat) on a state highway interchange
short_quote: Bleeding and flushing occur when hot weather causes the asphalt binder to expand onto the pavement surface,
source: TTI Pavements: 'Get a Grip - New Fine PFC Offsets Bleeding, Flushing on Roadways' (Aug 6, 2013), read on the Lufkin TxDOT District tag page

claim: TxDOT's Seal Coat Manual (flushing page) calls too much binder one of the most common defects. The excess rises to the surface and makes the black, often sticky condition called flushing, bleeding or fattening up, which can lead to a loss of skid resistance. It also says a poorly designed and constructed seal coat can begin its life with a surface so flushed that it shows a loss of skid characteristics.
surfaces: seal coats and surface treatments
short_quote: a surface that may have flushed so badly that it will exhibit a loss of skid characteristics
source: TxDOT Seal Coat and Surface Treatment Manual, Ch. 1 Sec. 4: Principal Faults or Defects - Flushing

claim: TxDOT defines short-term aggregate loss as stone lost within hours or days after construction. Among the causes it lists for loss within a few days is cold weather right after construction. In its broader list of major causes of serious stone loss, it includes fast traffic before adhesion is fully developed and a rainstorm before adhesion develops, and it says seal coats tend to perform better if they are under traffic a few months before winter. Its McLeod design method allows for traffic whip-off: about 5% for low-volume, residential traffic and 10% for higher-speed roadways.
numbers: Whip-off wastage: 5% for low-volume residential traffic, 10% for higher-speed roads
surfaces: newly placed seal coats / surface treatments
short_quote: Short-term aggregate loss refers to aggregate loss within hours or days after construction.
source: TxDOT Seal Coat and Surface Treatment Manual (revised September 2024), Ch. 1 Sec. 4, Ch. 2 Sec. 3, Ch. 4 Sec. 2 (full PDF)

claim: TxDOT limits seal coats mainly to low-traffic roads. It counts any road above 10,000 vehicles a day as high traffic. Problems on busier roads include early stone loss, vehicle damage from loose stone (windshields, headlights, radiators, paint), possible flushing, tire noise and long traffic control. The manual says to be cautious using seal coats in urban areas with frequent speeding up, slowing down and turning. Letting only slow-moving traffic onto a new seal coat after sweeping is one of the best ways to reduce early stone loss.
numbers: High traffic = ADT over 10,000 vehicles per day
surfaces: seal coats on low- vs high-volume roads (e.g. farm-to-market vs urban arterials)
short_quote: Facilities with average daily traffic in excess of 10,000 vehicles per day will be considered as high traffic for purposes of this manual.
source: TxDOT Seal Coat and Surface Treatment Manual (revised September 2024), Ch. 2 Sec. 3: Traffic Volume Considerations for Seal Coat Treatment

claim: On rural Texas horizontal curves, wet-weather crash frequency depends strongly on both pavement skid resistance and annual rainfall. The study covered five years of crash data and included seal coat (chip seal) among the surfaces tested. Every surface loses skid resistance over time through traffic polishing and weather wear, at different rates by treatment and aggregate type. The sites with the most to gain are most likely in the rainiest parts of the state and on pavements needing resurfacing, such as flushed seal coats.
numbers: Five years of crash data analyzed
surfaces: rural highway curves; seal coat/chip seal, hot-mix asphalt, permeable friction course, high-friction surface treatment
short_quote: wet-weather crash frequency is highly sensitive to both pavement skid resistance and annual precipitation rate.
source: TxDOT Project Summary 0-6932: Developing Pavement Safety-Based Guidelines for Improving Horizontal Curve Safety (TTI, completed 8-31-2018)

claim: This statewide Texas study (18,843 on-system roadbed miles, fiscal years 2021 to 2023, 24,873 crashes) built separate logistic crash-susceptibility models for asphalt with a surface treatment, asphalt without one, CRCP and jointed concrete. AADT and precipitation were positively associated with crash likelihood on every pavement type, and skid number (and roughness) were significant in most cases. Pothole presence was positively associated with crashes only on surface-treated asphalt. Rut depth, raveling, flushing and failures on asphalt (and punchouts on CRCP) showed no significant effect. Recommended thresholds are MPD of 0.03 in and SN of 40. Of 627 hydroplaning crashes found by a language model reading crash narratives, 90% occurred at model-averaged water film thickness below 0.05 in, against the traditional 0.095 in threshold.
numbers: 18,843 roadbed miles; FY2021-2023; 24,873 crashes; 627 hydroplaning crashes; MPD > 0.03 in; SN > 40; 90% of hydroplaning crashes at WFT < 0.05 in (vs 0.095 in traditional threshold)
surfaces: asphalt with surface treatment, asphalt without surface treatment, CRCP, jointed concrete (Texas on-system roads)
short_quote: rut depth, raveling, flushing, and failures for ACP and punchout for CRCP showed no significant effect on crash susceptibility
source: TxDOT Project Summary 0-7177: Identifying Pavement Improvement Projects for Enhanced Safety (TTI / University of Houston, completed 4-3-2026)

claim: Seal coats in Texas are redone on a short cycle. The average life of a seal coat or surface treatment is about six to eight years, though some have lasted up to 20. TxDOT says a 6 to 8 year cycle is desirable but not always possible because of funding. Contractors place 17,000 to 20,000 lane miles a year and TxDOT crews about 3,000 to 4,000, and seal coats are a very important part of TxDOT's preventive maintenance program.
numbers: Average life 6 to 8 years (some up to 20); 17,000-20,000 contracted + 3,000-4,000 state-force lane miles per year
surfaces: seal coats / surface treatments on Texas state-maintained roads, mostly lower-volume
short_quote: The average life of a seal coat or surface treatment is about six to eight years
source: TxDOT Seal Coat and Surface Treatment Manual (revised September 2024), Ch. 1 Sec. 1 and Ch. 2

claim: The NTSB found that the Feb 11, 2021 crash in the southbound toll lanes of I-35W in Fort Worth (about 6:00 a.m. CST) was caused by ice building up on the surface of the elevated roadway, which made drivers lose control. 130 vehicles were involved and six people were fatally injured. Before the crash the area had 36 consecutive hours below freezing, with light mist and fog reported from 2:53 to 4:53 a.m. The NTSB listed drivers going too fast for the winter weather as a contributing factor. The posted limit on the toll lanes was 75 mph.
numbers: 130 vehicles; 6 fatally injured; 36 consecutive hours below freezing; mist/fog 2:53-4:53 a.m.; posted limit 75 mph
surfaces: Elevated roadway / bridge structure on an interstate (I-35W toll lanes)
short_quote: ice accumulation on the surface of the elevated roadway, which made drivers lose control of their vehicles.
source: NTSB Investigation HWY21FH005: Multivehicle Crash on I-35W, Fort Worth, Texas

claim: NWS Fort Worth's summary of the February 2021 storm describes freezing drizzle that left a thin, nearly invisible ice glaze on many roads. Cars slid off the road, there were several crashes, and the 100+ car I-35W pileup happened. Snow, sleet and freezing rain followed (Feb 14-17). At DFW Airport the temperature stayed at or below freezing for 93 hours (5 pm Feb 9 to 2 pm Feb 13) and then 139 hours (5 pm Feb 13 to noon Feb 19). DFW got 5.0 inches of snow, and the low was -2 F on Feb 16. One caveat: the page dates the freezing-drizzle event Feb 11-12, but the pileup happened on the morning of Feb 11. For scoring: light freezing drizzle, not heavy snow, produced the deadliest road ice, and it fell days into a long freeze.
numbers: 93 hours and 139 hours at or below freezing at DFW; 5.0 in. event snowfall at DFW; -2 F low on Feb 16, 2021
surfaces: all
short_quote: Freezing drizzle occurred across much of the region which led to a thin coating of nearly invisible ice on many roadways.
source: NWS Fort Worth: February 2021 Winter Event summary

claim: The National Weather Service says bridges and overpasses freeze before other road surfaces. It describes black ice as patchy ice on roads that is hard to see. The page also says black ice can form when rain-wet roads drop below freezing overnight, so the hazard can come after the precipitation ends.
surfaces: Bridges and overpasses (compared with at-grade pavement)
short_quote: Bridges and overpasses are particularly dangerous because they freeze before other surfaces.
source: NWS Winter Safety: Ice and Frost

claim: TxDOT's winter driving guidance says bridges, ramps, overpasses and shaded areas tend to freeze first. It tells drivers to keep at least three times the normal following distance on snow or ice and strongly advises staying off the roads. Staying home lowers traffic volume, which matters when reading daily crash counts on ice days.
numbers: 3x normal following distance
surfaces: Bridges, ramps, overpasses, shaded areas on state roads
short_quote: Use extra caution on bridges, ramps, overpasses, and shaded areas as they tend to freeze first.
source: TxDOT: Snow and ice - winter weather driving tips

claim: A Utah DOT / BYU study measured surface temperatures where an asphalt and a concrete pavement meet on U.S. 40 near Heber, Utah. Concrete reached freezing before asphalt in every time period except late afternoon, so on average asphalt would need less winter maintenance. The authors warn that results depend on each site's materials and conditions. The site is a cold mountain location in Utah, not North Texas.
surfaces: Portland cement concrete vs asphalt (at-grade)
short_quote: concrete pavement will experience freezing before asphalt pavement for all time periods except late afternoon
source: Comparison of wintertime asphalt and concrete pavement surface temperatures on U.S. Route 40 near Heber, Utah (Guthrie, Bytheway, Dye, Eggett; UDOT report UT-14.03, 2014)

claim: An earlier BYU thesis by one of the same authors found no clear winner. Near freezing, asphalt did better in the afternoon and concrete did better at other times of day. The two were equally likely to collect snow or ice and need equal maintenance on average. Taken together with the 2014 study, the evidence for a concrete vs asphalt difference in freezing weather is mixed and site-specific. Any surface effect on ice days should be treated as uncertain.
surfaces: Portland cement concrete vs asphalt
short_quote: Asphalt and concrete are equally likely to collect snow or ice on their surfaces
source: Comparison of Winter Temperature Profiles in Asphalt and Concrete Pavements (Jeremy B. Dye, BYU thesis, 2010)

claim: A peer-reviewed US study of snowfalls found fewer fatal crashes on snow days than on dry days (IRR 0.93), but more nonfatal-injury crashes (IRR 1.23) and more property-damage-only crashes (IRR 1.45). The first snowy day of the year was more deadly than other snow days (IRR 1.14), and especially so for elderly drivers (IRR 1.34). The authors say traffic falls 7% to 56% in snow according to other studies. Assuming a 29% drop, they estimate a per-traveler fatality risk 18% higher than on dry days. For scoring: raw counts understate per-trip risk, and the first winter-weather day of a season deserves extra weight.
numbers: Fatal IRR 0.93; nonfatal-injury IRR 1.23; PDO IRR 1.45; first snow day fatal IRR 1.14 (elderly 1.34); traffic volume decrease 7%-56%; fatality risk 18% higher assuming 29% traffic reduction
surfaces: all
short_quote: The first snowy day of the year was substantially more dangerous than other snow days in terms of fatalities
source: Eisenberg & Warner, Effects of Snowfalls on Motor Vehicle Collisions, Injuries, and Fatalities, American Journal of Public Health 2005;95(1):120-124

claim: On seven Iowa interstate segments, winter storm events (4+ hours, at least 0.51 cm/hr of snow) cut traffic volume by about 29% on average (95% CI 22.3 to 35.8%). The average cut ranged from about 16% to 47% by location and had a significant positive relationship with total snowfall and the square of maximum gust wind speed. The storm crash rate was 5.86 crashes per million vehicle-km against 0.41 in non-storm periods, about 1,300% higher. These rates are for comparison only, because ATR volumes do not represent the whole segment. On average 2 crashes were reported per storm event vs 0.65 in comparable non-storm periods, though the non-storm figure covers a longer time. The authors say several factors could explain the rate gap: the severe conditions themselves, much lower volumes (a few crashes on little traffic give a high rate), and possible over-reporting of crashes in bad weather.
numbers: Average volume reduction ~29% (range ~16-47%; 95% CI 22.3-35.8%); storm crash rate 5.86 vs non-storm 0.41 crashes per million vehicle-km (~1,300% difference); avg 2 crashes per storm event vs 0.65 in comparable periods
surfaces: Rural interstates (Iowa)
short_quote: The average winter storm volume reduction was approximately 29 percent, but ranged from approximately 16 to 47 percent.
source: Knapp, Smithson & Khattak, The Mobility and Safety Impacts of Winter Storm Events in a Freeway Environment, Mid-Continent Transportation Symposium Proceedings (Iowa State University, c. 2000)

claim: Weather is linked to about 1 in 8 US crashes, and rain (including mist) is by far the biggest weather cause. FHWA puts it at over three quarters of weather-related crashes and injuries, against about 1% for severe crosswinds. FHWA's current page no longer gives a separate wet-pavement crash figure. Rain also changes traffic itself: speeds on signalized arterials drop 10 to 25% on wet pavement, and freeway speed variance can fall 25% in rain.
numbers: 2019-2023 five-year average: 744,911 weather-related crashes a year (12% of crashes), 268,239 injured (11%), 3,807 killed (9%). Rain/mist: 574,047 crashes (10% of all crashes), 219,039 injured (82% of weather-related injuries), 2,810 killed (74% of weather-related fatalities). Severe crosswinds: 5,870 crashes (0.1%), 2,426 injured, 65 killed (2% of weather-related fatalities). Wet-pavement speed reduction on arterials 10-25%. Note: the table's '7% of weather-related crashes' for rain looks like a typo, since 574,047/744,911 is about 77%.
surfaces: all (national, all road types; no surface breakdown)
short_quote: Over 77 percent of most weather-related crashes happen during rain or mist conditions.
source: FHWA Road Weather Management Program: How Do Weather Events Impact Roads?

claim: Low visibility (fog, smog, smoke, blowing dust or sand) is rare but deadly for how rare it is. It accounts for about 4% of weather-related crashes but 13% of weather-related deaths. FHWA says it cuts traffic speed by 10 to 12% and freeway capacity by 12%. That makes it a separate, high-severity signal rather than just a smaller version of rain.
numbers: 2019-2023 average: 32,871 crashes a year (1% of all crashes, 4% of weather-related), 11,292 injured, 488 killed (13% of weather-related fatalities). Speed reduction 10-12%. Freeway capacity reduced 12%.
surfaces: all (national; freeway capacity figure is for freeways)
short_quote: Low visibility can cause speed reductions of 10 to 12 percent.
source: FHWA Road Weather Management Program: How Do Weather Events Impact Roads?

claim: FHWA's fog page gives a fog-only count, larger than the low-visibility category in the 2019-2023 table (the period and definitions differ, and the page gives no date range). It names greater speed variance, meaning drivers slowing by different amounts, as the reason crash risk goes up.
numbers: Over 38,700 fog crashes a year, over 600 killed, more than 16,300 injured (undated).
surfaces: all
short_quote: Low visibility conditions cause increased speed variance, which increases crash risk.
source: FHWA Road Weather Management Program: Low Visibility

claim: Fog and smoke (FS) crashes in Florida (2003-2007) were most common on winter mornings (December to February). Compared with clear-visibility crashes, they tended to cause more severe injuries and involve more vehicles. Head-on and rear-end were the two most common crash types in both risk and severity. They were more common on high-speed roads, undivided roads, roads without sidewalks and two-lane rural roads, and more likely at night without street lights, where injuries were also more severe. (Our inference, not the paper's: weight fog risk toward high-speed, undivided and rural two-lane roads such as farm-to-market roads.)
numbers: Florida crash data 2003-2007; peak season Dec-Feb mornings (no relative-risk figure in the abstract).
surfaces: high-speed roads, undivided roads, two-lane rural roads (no pavement-surface breakdown)
short_quote: FS-related crashes tend to result in more severe injuries and involve more vehicles.
source: Abdel-Aty, Ekram, Huang, Choi (2011), A study on crashes related to visibility obstruction due to fog and smoke, Accident Analysis and Prevention 43(5):1730-1737

claim: Using 5-minute, 0.01-degree radar (NEXRAD) matched to 125,012 US fatal crashes (crashes involving alcohol or drugs left out), the relative risk of a fatal crash was 1.343 (95% CI 1.315-1.371) while precipitation was falling. That is precipitation of any type: radar could not tell rain from snow. Risk was 1.29 (CI 1.26-1.32) in light precipitation (<2.5 mm/h) and 2.46 (CI 2.29-2.63) in heavy precipitation (>7.6 mm/h). The text also gives 1.27 for light at one point. Precipitation risk ran from about 1.0 overnight to a peak of 1.6 in the morning rush hour. By region it ran from 1.22 (Northeast) to 1.74 (Northern Rockies). Precipitation was falling in 7.7% of fatal crashes, against 5.8% of the time in the climatology. The authors say 'a great deal of the risk due to precipitation is applicable only while it is actively falling, rather than afterward.' They also say very heavy rates 'are often washed out by aggregating to longer time scales', which implies daily totals understate the risk of short downpours.
numbers: Overall RR 1.343 (95% CI 1.315-1.371). Light (<2.5 mm/h) RR 1.29 (CI 1.26-1.32); the text also says 1.27 at one point. Heavy (>7.6 mm/h) RR 2.46 (CI 2.29-2.63). Morning rush peak about 1.6. Regional range 1.22 (Northeast) to 1.74 (Northern Rockies). Rain was falling in 7.7% of fatal crashes vs 5.8% climatology.
surfaces: all (fatal crashes only, alcohol/drug cases excluded; no surface breakdown)
short_quote: risk increases more dramatically with heavier precipitation, nearly doubling from 1.27 during light precipitation to 2.46 during heavy precipitation
source: Stevens, Schreck, Saha, Bell, Kunkel (2019), Precipitation and Fatal Motor Vehicle Crashes: Continental Analysis with High-Resolution Radar Data, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, DOI 10.1175/BAMS-D-18-0001.1

claim: On a daily scale, which matches our model, rainy days raised crash rates about 10% and injury rates about 8% across six US states (1996-2010). The jump grew with the day's rain total, to +51% crashes and +38% injuries on days with more than 50 mm (2 in.). Urban counties saw the biggest rise in relative risk, but rural counties with and without interstates also rose. That supports a dose-response rain term and a larger urban effect.
numbers: Rain days: +10% crashes, +8% injuries. Days with >50 mm rain: +51% crashes, +38% injuries. States: Arkansas, Georgia, Illinois, Maryland, Minnesota, Ohio, 1996-2010. The search summary also mentioned about 28,000 extra crashes a year in May-September, but that line is not among the quotes I verified.
surfaces: all (urban vs rural counties; with vs without interstates; no pavement-surface breakdown)
short_quote: an overall increase in crashes and injuries of 51% and 38% during days with more than 50 mm (2 in.) of rainfall
source: Black, Villarini, Mote (2017), Effects of Rainfall on Vehicle Crashes in Six U.S. States, Weather, Climate, and Society 9(1):53-70, DOI 10.1175/WCAS-D-16-0035.1

claim: Merging NOAA Storm Events records with the DOT's FARS fatality data found 232 deaths from windblown dust events in 2007-2017. That is far more than NOAA's Natural Hazard Statistics report, partly because those statistics assign some dust fatalities to high winds and thunderstorms (about 45%). Deaths cluster in the Southwest, for example the I-10 'Deadliest 10 Miles' between Phoenix and Tucson and Lordsburg Playa in New Mexico. The deadliest wrecks involved semi trucks, and five of the six deadliest were dust storms on I-10. The authors call dust an underappreciated hazard.
numbers: 232 deaths, 2007-2017. About 45% of dust fatalities assigned by NOAA statistics to high winds and thunderstorms.
surfaces: all (mostly highways and interstates in the Southwest)
short_quote: There was a total of 232 deaths from windblown dust events from 2007 to 2017.
source: Tong, Feng, Gill, Schepanski, Wang (2023), How Many People Were Killed by Windblown Dust Events in the United States?, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society 104(5):E1067-E1084, DOI 10.1175/bams-d-22-0186.1

claim: Fine-particle air pollution (PM2.5, the main part of smoke haze) raised daily crash involvement in the UK. The study used temperature inversions to separate pollution from driving behavior. Each extra 1 microgram per cubic meter of PM2.5 added 0.3 to 0.6% to the number of vehicles in crashes that day. This is general air pollution, not wildfire smoke, so it is weak support for a haze term.
numbers: +0.3% to +0.6% vehicles involved in accidents per day per +1 ug/m3 PM2.5; UK 2009-2014.
surfaces: all
short_quote: We find an increase of 0.3 − 0.6% in the number of vehicles involved in accidents per day
source: Sager (2019), Estimating the effect of air pollution on road safety using atmospheric temperature inversions, Journal of Environmental Economics and Management 98

claim: Rain and snow slow traffic and cut throughput on freeways, and the effect grows with intensity. Light rain or snow cuts average freeway speed 3-13%, heavy rain 3-16%, heavy snow 5-40%. Maximum flow drops about 14% in heavy rain and 30-44% in heavy snow. On arterials, speeds fall 10-25% on wet pavement and 30-40% on snowy or slushy pavement, and arterial volumes can fall 15-30% depending on conditions and time of day. FHWA also says about 12% of crashes (about 745,000 a year) are weather-related, and over 77% of those happen in rain or mist.
numbers: Freeway avg speed: light rain/snow -3 to -13%; heavy rain -3 to -16%; heavy snow -5 to -40%. Max flow: -14% heavy rain; -30 to -44% heavy snow. Capacity: light rain -4 to 11; heavy rain -10 to -30%; heavy snow -12 to -27%. Arterial speed: -10 to -25% wet, -30 to -40% snowy/slushy; arterial volume -15 to -30%. 12% of crashes weather-related (~745,000); >77% of those in rain/mist.
surfaces: all; freeways and arterials (not split by pavement type)
short_quote: Heavy rain can decrease average speed by 3 to 16 percent.
source: How Do Weather Events Impact Roads? (FHWA Road Weather Management Program)

claim: Light rain barely changes how many vehicles use the road: FHWA notes 'little or no effect on flow' under light rain. Heavy rain cuts flow by about 10-20% (Ibrahim and Hall 1994). Snow cuts volume much more, and the drop grows with snowfall. Under 25 mm: 7-17% on weekdays, 19-31% on weekends. 25-75 mm: 11-25% / 30-41%. 75-150 mm: 18-34% / 39-47% (Hanbali and Kuemmel 1992). Weekday drops are smaller, likely because most weekday trips are nondiscretionary. Studies on the page put heavy-rain capacity loss at 14-15% (Ibrahim and Hall) or 25-30% (Smith et al. 2004), and light-rain capacity loss at 4-10% (Smith et al.).
numbers: Heavy rain flow reduction 10-20% (Ibrahim and Hall 1994). Light rain: little or no effect on flow. Snow <25 mm: -7 to -17% weekdays, -19 to -31% weekends; 25-75 mm: -11 to -25% / -30 to -41%; 75-150 mm: -18 to -34% / -39 to -47% (Hanbali and Kuemmel 1992). Free-flow speed: light rain -2 to -3.6%, rain -6 to -9%; capacity -10 to -11% in rain regardless of intensity.
surfaces: all; mainly freeways
short_quote: Little or no effect on flow was observed under light rain conditions.
source: Empirical Studies on Traffic Flow in Inclement Weather (FHWA), Executive Summary and Section 2

claim: Measured at a Melbourne site, wet days cut daily traffic volume by only a few percent: about 1.4% in winter and 2.1% in spring, reaching 2-3% for 2-10 mm days. This matches FHWA's finding that light-to-moderate rain removes few vehicles, so a daily crash count on a rain day mostly reflects higher per-vehicle risk, not lower exposure.
numbers: -1.35% (winter) and -2.11% (spring) on wet days; 2-3% over the 2-10 mm range; largest -3.43% for 2-5 mm days in spring; daytime rainfall -1.86% winter, -2.16% spring
surfaces: all (one urban count site, Melbourne, Australia)
short_quote: There are statistically significant decreases of 1.35 and 2.11% in traffic volume on wet days in winter and spring.
source: Keay and Simmonds (2005), The association of rainfall and other weather variables with road traffic volume in Melbourne, Australia, Accident Analysis and Prevention (abstract on University of Melbourne page)

claim: The risk of a fatal crash climbs steeply with rain intensity. Using radar at the crash's place and time for 125,012 US fatal crashes (2006-2011), the study found light precipitation raised fatal-crash risk about 27-29% and heavy precipitation about 2.5 times. Overall the rise was 34%, highest in the morning rush hour and in winter. Daily totals blur this: a daily-scale study found only a 1.47 relative risk on days over 20 mm. A model using daily DFW rain will understate heavy-burst risk. The risk ratios compare crash-time weather with that place's usual weather, not with traffic counts.
numbers: Overall RR 1.343 (95% CI 1.315-1.371). Light (<2.5 mm/h) RR 1.27-1.29; heavy (>7.6 mm/h) RR 2.46 (CI 2.29-2.63); moderate 2.5-7.6 mm/h. Regional RR 1.22 (Northeast) to 1.74 (Northern Rockies). Daily heavy-precip days (>20 mm) RR 1.47 (Hambly et al. 2013, cited). Prior literature range 1.10-1.76.
surfaces: all
short_quote: the risk of a fatal crash during heavy precipitation found to be more than double the background risk [RR = 2.46, CI = (2.29, 2.63)]
source: Stevens, Schreck, Saha, Bell and Kunkel (2019), Precipitation and Fatal Motor Vehicle Crashes: Continental Analysis with High-Resolution Radar Data, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society (NOAA Institutional Repository copy)

claim: Rain raises nonfatal crashes far more than fatal ones. On a given day, each centimeter of precipitation raises fatal-crash risk about 1% (fatal data: over 1 million crashes, 48 states, 1975-2000) and nonfatal-crash risk about 11% (nonfatal data: 36.4 million crashes, 17 states, 1990-1999). Risk also rises with time since the last rain. If it has been 2 days since the last rain, deadly-crash risk rises 3.7%; after 21 days, 9.2%. At the monthly level, an extra 10 cm of rain is linked to a 3.7% lower fatal crash rate.
numbers: Per cm of precipitation on a day: fatal +~1%, nonfatal +11%. After 2 dry days: +3.7% fatal-crash risk; after 21 days: +9.2%. Monthly: +10 cm rain linked to -3.7% fatal crash rate.
surfaces: all
short_quote: for nonfatal crashes, the increased risk is 11 percent
source: UC Berkeley News (2003), news release on Eisenberg, The mixed effects of precipitation on traffic crashes, Accident Analysis and Prevention

claim: Snow days show the 'more crashes, fewer deaths' pattern clearly. Compared with dry days, snow days had 7% fewer fatal crashes but 23% more injury crashes and 45% more property-damage-only crashes. The first snowy day of the year was more deadly than later snow days (IRR 1.14), especially for elderly drivers. Traffic volume has been shown to fall 7-56% in snow, so per-driver risk is higher than raw counts show. The authors credit slower, more careful driving for the lower severity. For DFW the parallel is freezing days: more total crashes, not necessarily more deaths, with the first icy day of a season likely worst.
numbers: Fatal IRR 0.93 (95% CI 0.90-0.97); nonfatal injury IRR 1.23 (1.18-1.29); PDO IRR 1.45 (1.38-1.52); first snowy day fatal IRR 1.14 (1.08-1.21); elderly 1.34 (1.23-1.50); traffic volume -7% to -56% in snow (cited)
surfaces: all
short_quote: Snow days had fewer fatal crashes than dry days
source: Eisenberg and Warner (2005), Effects of Snowfalls on Motor Vehicle Collisions, Injuries, and Fatalities, American Journal of Public Health (PMC)

claim: On Wisconsin interstates, among multi-vehicle crashes in rain, deeper estimated water film depth at the crash moment lowered the odds that a crash was fatal or incapacitating (backward sequential logit, stage one: coefficient -17.729, S.E. 8.5817, p = 0.0388). The authors read this as drivers seeing the risk and adjusting. In the chosen model, more travel lanes and straight (tangent) sections also lowered severity. In the forward-format model, vertical and horizontal/vertical curves raised the odds of fatal and incapacitating crashes. The sample is small: 536 crashes, only 13 of them fatal or incapacitating. Pavement surface type was a candidate input but was not among the significant predictors.
numbers: Water film depth coefficient -17.729 (S.E. 8.5817, p = 0.0388) in backward sequential logit, stage one; categories <0.02, 0.02-0.10, >0.1 mm/h
surfaces: interstate highways (Wisconsin); pavement type not separated
short_quote: fatal and incapacitating injury crashes decreased as water film depth increased
source: Jung, Qin and Noyce (2010), Injury Severity of Multi-Vehicle Crash in Rainy Weather, TRB 2010 Annual Meeting paper (University of Wisconsin-Madison TOPS Lab)
url: https://files.topslab.wisc.edu/publications/2010/INJURY SEVERITY OF MULTI-VEHICLE CRASH IN RAINY WEATHER (10-4056).pdf

claim: Holiday crash effects found in the literature are about deaths, and they depend on the holiday. July 4 has more US crash deaths than any other day, linked to alcohol. January 1 has the most pedestrian deaths and the fifth most deaths overall, also alcohol-related. High counts on other holidays are put down to more holiday or recreational travel. Summer and fall have more deaths than winter and spring, mainly because people drive more. This is fatal-only, US data from 1986 to 2002, so it does not say whether total (mostly minor) crashes rise or fall on holidays. Holidays with less commuting may have fewer total crashes even when deaths rise.
numbers: US averages >100 crash deaths per day; single-day range 45 to 252 (1986-2002); January 1 ranks fifth in deaths per day
surfaces: all
short_quote: On other days the high numbers of deaths are likely due to increases in holiday or recreational travel.
source: Farmer and Williams (2005), Temporal factors in motor vehicle crash deaths, Injury Prevention (PMC)

claim: TxDOT's own CRIS Public Extract File Specification (2018-and-later public extract, workbook dated 06/13/25 on TxDOT's crash data page) defines Surf_Type_ID as the road surface type at the crash location, filled only for crashes on the state highway system. Its source column is CRASH_ROAD_FACT.SURF_TYPE_ID, it is decoded with SURF_TYPE_LKP, and it runs from 2003 on. This supports limiting the project to state-maintained roads: city streets will have no code.
surfaces: all (state highway system only)
short_quote: Surf_Type_ID - The road surface type (concrete, blacktop, etc) at the location of the crash, for crashes located on the state highway system
source: TxDOT CRIS Public Extract File Specification (public-extract-file-specification.xlsx), 'Crash File Specification' sheet

claim: The official CRIS lookup does NOT match the codes in the newer data. The SURF_TYPE_LKP sheet in that same TxDOT workbook lists only six old codes, each marked effective from 1990-01-01 with no end date: 1 road is unpaved, 2 low type bituminous surface-treated, 3 intermediate type mixed, 4 high type flexible, 5 high type rigid, 6 high type composite. It has no codes 7 or 10. Under this lookup, 5 would mean rigid (concrete), which conflicts with the newer meaning (medium asphalt). So surf_type_id must not be decoded with CRIS's own lookup. The BASE_TYPE_LKP sheet is old in the same way (codes 1, 2, 3, 8, 9 only).
numbers: 6 codes (1-6); effective begin serial 32874 = 1990-01-01, end serial 2958465 = 9999-12-31
surfaces: all
short_quote: LOW TYPE BITUMINOUS SURFACE-TREATED | INTERMEDIATE TYPE MIXED | HIGH TYPE FLEXIBLE | HIGH TYPE RIGID | HIGH TYPE COMPOSITE
source: TxDOT CRIS Public Extract File Specification, 'SURF_TYPE_LKP' sheet

claim: The codes in the newer data match TxDOT's Roadway Inventory field SRF_TYPE ('Updated codes for YE2017'). In that scheme codes 1-4 are 1 continuously reinforced concrete, 2 jointed reinforced concrete, 3 jointed plain concrete and 4 thick asphalt (over 5.5 inches). This matches the project's decoding of 1-4, which was checked against Lewisville.
numbers: code 4 = over 5.5 inches
surfaces: concrete (CRCP, JRCP, JPCP), thick asphalt
short_quote: 1=Continuously Reinforced Concrete 2=Jointed Reinforced Concrete 3=Jointed Plain Concrete 4=Thick Asphaltic Concrete, over 5.5 inches
source: TxDOT Roadway Inventory File Format (RIF), Effective for YE2023 - Current, Date Revised 09/03/2024, item 5.23 SURFACE-TYPE / SRF_TYPE (TPP-DM-RIB). Copy hosted on a UT Austin course page, not txdot.gov

claim: In the same official SRF_TYPE list, code 5 is medium asphalt (2.5 to 5.5 inches) and code 6 is thin asphalt (under 2.5 inches). This confirms the project's guesses of 'intermediate asphalt' for 5 and 'thin asphalt' for 6, with TxDOT calling 5 'Medium'. The same document records that the descriptions for codes 5 and 6 were reversed in the YE2009 revision. The data's year matters, but 2020 to 2024 falls under the current scheme.
numbers: 5 = 2.5-5.5 inches; 6 = under 2.5 inches
surfaces: intermediate/medium asphalt, thin asphalt
short_quote: 5=Medium Asphaltic Concrete, 2.5 - 5.5 inches 6=Thin Asphaltic Concrete, under 2.5 inches
source: TxDOT Roadway Inventory File Format (RIF), YE2023 - Current, item 5.23 SRF_TYPE

claim: In the official SRF_TYPE list, code 7 is composite (asphalt over concrete) and code 10 is surface treatment pavement, which confirms the project's 'thin-surfaced or seal coat' reading of 10. The list also has codes the project's grouping does not mention: 8 widened composite, 9 overlaid and widened asphalt, 11 brick, 12 bladed and 13 gravel (all three unpaved), and 99 unknown. The project should assert that 8, 9, 11-13 and 99 are absent from the data, or else put 8 with composite, 9 with asphalt, and drop the unpaved codes and 99.
surfaces: asphalt over concrete, surface treatment / seal coat, widened/overlaid, unpaved
short_quote: 7=Composite (Asphalt Surfaced Concrete) 8=Widened Composite Pavement 9=Overlaid and Widened Asphaltic Concrete Pavement 10=Surface Treatment Pavement
source: TxDOT Roadway Inventory File Format (RIF), YE2023 - Current, item 5.23 SRF_TYPE

claim: The revision log, under 'Revisions for YE2017' (page 29), shows SRF_TYPE moving from the old scheme to the current one. 'Previous': 1 road is unpaved, 2 low type bituminous surface-treated, 3 intermediate type mixed, 4 high type flexible, 5 high type rigid, 6 high type composite, plus 99 unknown. 'Update': the new 1-13 plus 99 list. Item 5.23 is marked '(Updated codes for YE2017)'. Codes 1-6 of the 'Previous' list match CRIS's SURF_TYPE_LKP, which has no 99. So CRIS appears to copy SRF_TYPE from the roadway inventory without updating its published lookup. That is an inference; TxDOT does not say it.
numbers: YE2017 code update
surfaces: all
short_quote: SRF_TYPE Previous: 1 = Road is unpaved (unpaved) Update: 1 = Continuously Reinforced Concrete
source: TxDOT Roadway Inventory File Format (RIF), revision history pages 29-30

claim: TxDOT's 2003 PMIS guide, Table 1 'PMIS Pavement Types (Broad and Detail)', uses a 1-10 detailed pavement type list. Codes 1-7 and 10 match the current SRF_TYPE meanings closely. Codes 8 and 9 are worded a little differently: PMIS 8 'Overlaid or Widened Old Concrete Pavement' and 9 'Overlaid or Widened Old Flexible Pavement'. It defines 10 as 'Thin-surfaced Flexible Base Pavement (surface treatment or seal coat)'. Its note says Pavement Type 5 is the default for all PMIS Data Collection Sections, and that unrated or new sections get 5 'even for concrete pavements'. This is stated for PMIS only. The document calls type 7 'Composite Pavement (heavily-stabilized asphalt-surfaced pavement)', while the current SRF_TYPE list says 'Composite (Asphalt Surfaced Concrete)'.
numbers: Type 4 >5.5 in; Type 5 2.5-5.5 in; Type 6 <2.5 in
surfaces: surface treatment / seal coat; intermediate asphalt (default-value caveat)
short_quote: Pavement Type 5 is the default value for all PMIS Data Collection Sections.
source: Managing Texas Pavements: Basic Concepts and Data Interpretation for TxDOT's Pavement Management Information System (PMIS), TxDOT, July 2003, Table 1 (hosted by UT CTR Library)

claim: A TTI study for TxDOT puts the asphalt-type PMIS codes into three performance families. Family A is thick ACP (4), intermediate ACP (5) and overlaid ACP (9). Family B is composite (7) and concrete overlaid with ACP (8). Family C is thin ACP (6) and thin-surfaced ACP (10). This backs the project's choice to keep 7 apart from plain asphalt. It also suggests an alternative grouping: put 6 with 10 as 'thin surfaces' rather than with 4 and 5.
numbers: 3 families over 7 ACP types (4-10)
surfaces: all asphalt-type surfaces incl. composite and surface-treated
short_quote: Pavement Family C: This pavement family includes thin ACP (PMIS Pavement Type 6) and thin-surfaced ACP (PMIS Pavement Type 10).
source: Evaluation and Development of Pavement Scores, Performance Models and Needs Estimates for the TxDOT PMIS - Final Report, FHWA/TX-12/0-6386-3, Texas A&M Transportation Institute, Oct 2012
